title: THE FIRST THORNS GREW AFTER MAN SINNED. THEN THEY PUT THEM ON JESUS’ HEAD.
paragraphs:
THE FIRST THORNS GREW AFTER MAN SINNED. THEN THEY PUT THEM ON JESUS’ HEAD.
The soldiers thought they were humiliating a condemned King. But when you trace the thorns all the way back to Genesis, the crown becomes almost unbearable to look at.
There is something about the crown of thorns that we may have looked at a thousand times without truly seeing.
We see the paintings.
We see the blood.
We see the twisted branches pressed against the head of Jesus.
We know the scene so well that familiarity can make us move past it too quickly.
But go back.
Not to Pilate.
Not to Jerusalem.
Not even to Bethlehem.
Go all the way back to a garden.
Because long before Roman soldiers twisted thorns into a crown, Scripture had already introduced thorns into humanity’s story.
And the place where they first appear should make every Christian stop.
Adam has sinned.
Humanity has rebelled against God.
The innocence of Eden has been shattered.
Adam and Eve are hiding from the God whose presence they once enjoyed without fear.
Sin has entered the human story, and with sin come shame, alienation, pain, toil and death.
Then God speaks concerning the ground.
Genesis 3:18 contains these Hebrew words:
וְקוֹץ וְדַרְדַּר
weqots wedardar.
“Thorn and thistle.”
The earth that had been entrusted to humanity would now resist him.
“Thorns and thistles” would grow.
Read that slowly.
Before the crown of thorns appears in the Gospel story, thorns appear in Genesis in the aftermath of humanity’s rebellion.
They belong to the landscape of a world no longer experienced as Eden.
And thousands of years later...
Jesus is standing before Roman soldiers.
He has been scourged.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Humiliated.
And someone gets an idea.
Make the “King” a crown.
Matthew records what happened:
καὶ πλέξαντες στέφανον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν
kai plexantes stephanon ex akanthōn...
“and having twisted together a crown of thorns...”
The Greek word στέφανον — stephanon means a crown or wreath.
ἀκανθῶν — akanthōn means thorns.
They weave the branches together.
Then they put the crown on His head.
And suddenly there is a haunting biblical picture before us.
The thorns associated with humanity’s fallen world are resting upon the head of humanity’s Savior.
We should be careful here.

The Bible does not explicitly tell us that the Roman soldiers chose thorns because of Genesis 3. They were mocking Jesus’ claim to kingship. They clothed Him in royal colors, gave Him a mock scepter, bowed sarcastically and hailed Him as “King of the Jews.”
They meant humiliation.
But the biblical echo is difficult to miss.
Genesis gives us thorns after human rebellion.
The Gospels give us the sinless Son of God wearing thorns as He moves toward the cross.
The soldiers thought they were staging a joke.
Heaven knew a King was going to His throne.
And maybe this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because Adam’s story is not merely Adam’s story.
It is ours.
We know what it is to reach for something God told us not to touch.
We know what it is to believe the whisper that our way will make us happier than obedience.
We know what it is to hide.
We know what it is to cover ourselves.
We know what it is to blame someone else.
We know what it is to smile in church while carrying something inside us that we desperately hope nobody discovers.
Different garden.
Same rebellion.
Different century.
Same human heart.
You may never have eaten forbidden fruit from a tree, but perhaps you have deleted messages so nobody would find them.
Perhaps you have opened something on your phone you would never open with Jesus visibly sitting beside you.
Perhaps bitterness has lived inside you so long that you stopped calling it bitterness and started calling it discernment.
Perhaps pride learned Christian vocabulary.
Perhaps lust learned how to worship on Sunday.
Perhaps greed learned how to call itself ambition.
Perhaps unforgiveness learned how to call itself boundaries.
Perhaps you know exactly how to lift your hands while keeping one locked room of your heart closed to Christ.
And sin always promises fruit.
Then eventually...
thorns.
That is Eden.
Humanity reaches for the fruit and inherits the thorns.
But the Gospel gives us a breathtaking reversal.
We produced the rebellion.
Christ bore the shame.
We deserved judgment.
Christ went willingly toward the cross.
We wandered.
The Shepherd came looking.
We hid from God.
God came for us.
And on the way to Calvary, the Son of God stood silently while sinful hands twisted thorns together and placed them upon His head.
Think about whose head they were touching.
The head of the One through whom all things were made.
The head of the One before whom angels worship.
The head of the One who spoke storms into silence.
The head of the One who touched lepers without becoming unclean.
The head of the One who welcomed sinners, confronted hypocrites, forgave the repentant, opened blind eyes and called dead men from graves.
They crowned Him with thorns.
Then they laughed.
“Hail, King of the Jews!”
They did not understand the King standing in front of them.
His kingdom was not built through Roman violence.
His victory would not come by escaping death.
His victory would come through entering it...
and defeating it.
Jesus did not stumble helplessly into Calvary.
He had already said that no one ultimately took His life from Him; He laid it down.
That changes the entire picture.
The crown was mockery.
The cross was execution.
The nails were real.
The suffering was real.
But Christ was not merely the helpless victim of circumstances.
He was the obedient Son giving Himself for sinners.
Paul later writes something staggering:
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν
Christos hēmas exēgorasen.
“Christ redeemed us.”
Galatians 3:13 declares that Christ redeemed His people from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.
Not because Jesus became sinful.
He remained the spotless Son of God.
But He bore the curse in our place.
He stood where guilty people deserved to stand.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
The innocent for the guilty.
The beloved Son carrying what rebels could never remove from themselves.
And now look again at the crown.
Thorns.
On Jesus.
Do you see why the image cuts so deeply?
The Bible begins with humanity losing paradise through rebellion against God.
It moves through generations of sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
Then the promised King comes.
And instead of receiving the honor He deserves, He is rejected by the people He came to save.
The King receives thorns.
The innocent One receives condemnation.
The Holy One walks toward criminals’ execution.
And eventually His blood falls to the ground.
The same earth upon which humanity has struggled beneath the consequences of the Fall now receives the blood of its Creator.
That is not sentimental Christianity.
That is scandalous grace.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin was never serious.
Look at Calvary and you will never be able to say sin does not matter.
Grace is costly.
Forgiveness is not God shrugging at evil.
At the cross, the holiness of God and the love of God are not enemies.
Justice is not ignored.
Sin is not renamed.
Jesus bears judgment for His people so that sinners who could never make themselves righteous can be reconciled to God through Him.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “be a better person.”
Better behavior cannot resurrect a spiritually dead heart.
Religion cannot erase guilt.
Church attendance cannot become your savior.
Your parents’ Christianity cannot become yours by inheritance.
A cross around your neck cannot substitute for Christ reigning in your heart.
You need Jesus.
Not Jesus added to the life you already decided to live.
Jesus as Lord.
Jesus as Savior.
Jesus as your righteousness.
Jesus as the One before whom the hidden doors finally open.
Because there is something else we often do with thorns.
We hide them.
We show people flowers.
We hide the thorns.
We post the smile.
We hide the addiction.
We quote Scripture.
We hide the bitterness.
We tell everybody God is good.
And He is.
But secretly we are exhausted because we have spent years trying to make sure nobody discovers the places where we are bleeding.
Jesus already knows.
And He still calls you.
Not into pretending.
Into repentance.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning.
It is agreeing with God about your sin and turning toward the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
You do not clean yourself enough to earn the cross.
You come because you cannot clean yourself.
You do not wait until you deserve grace.
Grace, by definition, is not deserved.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe underneath everything people know about you is one sentence you have been terrified to say:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Say it.
Not as engagement.
Not for appearance.
Not because somebody told you emotional words earn salvation.
They do not.
Come to Christ in genuine repentance and faith.
Tell Him the truth.
The entire truth.
The part you polished.
The part you buried.
The thing you promised would happen only once.
The resentment you have fed.
The secret compromise.
The spiritual numbness.
The years of pretending.
Bring it into His light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you can simply comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when hiding finally ends.
And if you are fighting your way back toward Christ after months or years of spiritual exhaustion, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
Someone reading the same words may realize they are not the only wounded believer refusing to walk away.
That is what the enemy wants isolated.
Shame says, “Hide.”
Grace says, “Come.”
The Gospel says there is mercy for sinners in Jesus Christ.
And the story does not end with a crown of thorns.
That matters.
Jesus was crucified.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
And on the third day...
the tomb could not keep Him.
The mocked King rose.
Death did not get the final sentence.
Sin did not get the final sentence.
Rome did not get the final sentence.
The grave did not get the final sentence.
Jesus did.
And the Bible ends with an extraordinary promise: the curse will not have the final word.
The story that began in a garden does not terminate in ruin.
God is making all things new.
That is Christian hope.
Not that this world will somehow repair itself if humanity becomes sufficiently enlightened.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
So perhaps you will never look at the crown of thorns quite the same way again.
When you see it, remember Genesis.
Remember what sin did.
Remember what rebellion cost.
Remember how far humanity fell.
But then remember Jesus.
Remember the King who stepped into our fallen world.
Remember the Savior who accepted mockery rather than abandoning His mission.
Remember the Lamb who went to the cross.
Remember the blood.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Christ.
That is why we say:
Because Scripture is filled with people whose lives looked disqualified until God’s mercy wrote something nobody expected.
Peter denied Him.
Grace was not finished.
Paul persecuted His church.
Grace was not finished.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer but faith in a dying King.
Grace was not finished.
And maybe...
grace is not finished with you either.
Do not confuse that with permission to remain in sin.
Grace does not merely comfort us while leaving our chains untouched.
The grace that forgives also teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Jesus did not die simply to make rebellion feel less frightening.
He saves people from sin and calls them to follow Him.
So repent.
Believe.
Come home.
And then live like someone whose King wore the thorns you could never remove yourself.
You may need to read it again on a night when shame starts whispering that you are beyond mercy.
Not as a transaction with God. We support Gospel work because grace has already been given to us, not because support buys grace.

But if Gospel Warrior is helping you see Scripture, confront sin, understand grace and grow closer to Jesus, you can help this ministry keep putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk through a church door.
Your share may put the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
Your tag may become somebody’s midnight reminder that Christ has not stopped calling them.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not merely admire the crown.
Come to the King.
Because one day the question will not be whether you shared a Christian article, owned Christian merchandise, followed a Christian page or knew Christian vocabulary.
The question underneath everything is far more personal:
What have you done with Jesus?
The soldiers gave Him thorns because they thought His kingship was a joke.
The resurrection revealed how terribly wrong they were.
And perhaps the most haunting picture to carry with you is this:
The world gave Jesus a crown made from the thorns of a fallen creation—and the King carried it all the way toward the cross to rescue fallen people like us.
Because the thorns were never the end of the story.
The King who wore them walked out of His grave.
